keyFindings.description: The architect's first required change, which I measured independently: the diagnostic for the one failure that announces nothing tells a role to read the workload's endpoints, and this identity has no grant there — `kubectl auth can-i get endpoints` and `list endpoints` both answer `no` from a role container holding the credential. The check for the silent failure would itself be refused. Drop the command; the symptom (the pod Ready while the published reachability block times out) and the label comparison the bullet already prints land a role on the cause without it.

The architect's second required change, measured here too: the naming clause says a second `apply` of a name in use "either fails on the Job's immutable fields or patches that role's workload". `kubectl auth can-i patch jobs` and `update jobs` both answer `no`, so it cannot patch another role's workload at all — it is refused `cannot patch resource "jobs"`. The other two consequences are real and the advice stands; the sentence wants what the cluster does.

The gate paragraph quotes an output no kubectl here produces, and an exit status that is mine to own: I reported `exit 0` last round from a pipeline, so what I measured was `head`'s status rather than `kubectl`'s, and the text took it. Measured properly, with the in-cluster configuration taken away: exit **1**, and the output is `The connection to the server localhost:8080 was refused - did you specify the right host or port?` — not `dial tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: connect: connection refused` plus `Warning: the server doesn't have a resource type 'jobs'`, which is what a different simulation (an emptied environment) prints. The paragraph's conclusion is right and its evidence is wrong; quote what a credential-less role gets, or state it without quoting.

The reachability check runs the instant `kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready` returns, and the pod template carries no readiness probe, so Ready means the container started. The example's image is `mirror.gcr.io/library/postgres:16`, whose entrypoint runs its whole initialisation with the TCP listener disabled before restarting the server, so at that moment the port is normally still closed and `socket.create_connection` fails at once with `ConnectionRefusedError`. The paragraph below names only the timeout and assigns it one cause — the missing reachability label — so the likeliest outcome of the published sequence has no reading offered, and the reading a role will reach for is wrong. Loop the connect for about a minute, and name the refusal as a server still starting. (The mechanism is read from the upstream entrypoint and the absent probe; the Service half cannot be driven here.)

The gate does not stop a role, and today every role reaches the stop. Before the declarations are applied the Service steps are refused `Forbidden` — the recorded state of this deployment — and the sequence is written unconditionally, so a role applies the Job, reads its uid, is refused, and only afterwards reads at :2620 that this was expected. The only `kubectl delete job` is below the step that failed, so the Job it started stays on a shared quota until its deadline. Say at the gate that unless both answers are a bare `yes` the role does not apply the Job; that also makes the paragraph at :2620-2621 unnecessary.

The delta amended the section opener to carry the exception and left the preamble directly above the bullets promising that each of them is "enforced in the namespace rather than in anyone's good behaviour" — the sentence a reader scanning the bullets actually meets, four lines above the bullet that says admission does not enforce it. One clause there.

"reading Services needs the same grant as creating them" is not how RBAC works: verbs are granted independently, and this identity in this namespace is the counterexample — `delete jobs` yes while `patch jobs` no. The conclusion (the last line asks only for Jobs and pods) is right because `get services` and `list services` both measure `no`, which is what the sentence should say.

All five test-phase proofs record `headSha` `63a5ab96903a95996e30bae1d0d8a7f2b15f5af5`, which does not exist — GitHub answers 422 for it. The commit is `63a5ab96903a68505eb288ad63a223398f13c7e1`, which `implement.json` cites correctly; the first twelve digits match and the rest is wrong, so no proof of that phase can be resolved by a later reader. The same handoff's private-name sweep describes its surface as "592 lines, five files" where that diff is nine files; the line count is exact and the file count understates it by the four handoffs, which are the files the sweep most needed to cover.

verified: All seven findings of the previous round are fixed, each checked rather than read: the namespace literal is redacted and appears nowhere on the branch; the reachability step is a python3 standard-library connect and `which psql` confirms why; the workload is named for its issue; the gate says neither answer is what a credential-less role gets; the label bullet is marked as the one rule admission does not enforce; the manifests are written outside the checkout; and the last line asks only for Jobs and pods.

Every other command the section names is within this identity's grant, measured from this role container: create/get/delete jobs, get and list pods, watch pods, get pods/log — all yes; create and get services, get and list endpoints, patch and update jobs, create pods — all no.
CI at code head 63a5ab96: 45 check runs, none unsuccessful, the required lint, typecheck, test and pr-title all success; compare 63a5ab96...5713433a is .legion/ only.

Considered and dismissed: that the workload's name should also carry `<project>`. An issue key carries its project's prefix, so `infra-71-postgres` is already unique among the projects of the deployment whose agents share that namespace and identity.
